Q1: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). The medic is a medical unit and Call A is both the highest-scored medical call and time-sensitive — a 68-year-old with chest pain is a potential cardiac event where minutes matter. Call B's ankle injury is non-life-threatening and the alarm activation isn't a medic task, so neither competes.
Q2: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Pine Rd, kitchen fire, 8.4). It's the higher score and, even with the family evacuated, a kitchen fire can spread to the structure or adjacent homes, so it carries the greater consequence if left. The dumpster fire at 7.9 is the next-in-queue once the engine clears or mutual aid arrives.
Q3: Dispatch the ladder to Call A (1st St, trapped person, 8.9). It edges out Call B by 0.1 and life-safety rescue — a person trapped in smoke on the 3rd floor — takes priority over an elevator rescue where occupants are contained and comparatively safe. Call B stays queued for the next available ladder or mutual-aid company.
Q4: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, 7.1). A conscious diabetic emergency is a legitimate medical call a BLS unit can treat and transport, and it clearly outranks a low-priority event standby at 5.5. If the event still needs standby coverage, the dispatcher can backfill or rely on another unit later.
Q5: Dispatch the medic to Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied, so the tiebreaker rule applies: respiratory distress is acutely time-sensitive and can deteriorate into arrest without warning, whereas the hip injury, though serious, is more stable. Call B stays first in queue for the next unit.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8) and accept the neighbor's mutual-aid offer for Call B (Side St, brush fire, 6.5). The vehicle fire scores slightly higher and a burning vehicle is a contained suppression task for my engine; sending mutual aid to the brush fire keeps both covered since brush near homes can escalate. This gets every waiting call a unit with no hold.
Q7: Dispatch the battalion chief to Call A (Park Ave, multi-vehicle accident, 7.5). It's the only call in the queue, the unit is the appropriate resource for command oversight, and holding it gains nothing. A multi-vehicle incident with injuries benefits from early command for scene coordination and incoming-unit tasking.
Q8: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). Stroke is a treatment-window emergency — the scored 8.7 already reflects that urgency, and the scenario notes the window is closing, which makes rapid transport to a stroke center decisive. Abdominal pain at 7.3, while real, is stable and waits for the next unit.
Q9: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Summit Dr, gas leak, 5.9). Holding a unit with a call waiting accomplishes nothing, and an evacuated home with a reported gas leak carries explosion and ignition risk that justifies a response despite the sub-critical score. The engine can confirm, secure, and hand off to the gas utility.
